title: Off-Roading
intro: Hop in your truck and drive to the national parks of the United States, from the glaciers of Alaska to the islands of the Caribbean!
milestones: You made it over the rocky pass!
You splashed across the shallow creek!
You reached the top of the switchbacks!
You drove through the tall pine forest!
You found a great lookout point!
You crossed the old wooden bridge!
You made it through the sandy wash!
You reached the campground by the lake!
You climbed the steep dirt road!
You can see the park entrance ahead!
detours: Oh no, a mudslide blocked the road! Solve {count} problems to winch the truck out.
A flat tire! Solve {count} problems to change it and get rolling again.
A herd of bison is crossing the road. Solve {count} problems while you wait for them to pass!
A fallen tree is in the way! Solve {count} problems to saw a path around it.
The truck is stuck in deep sand! Solve {count} problems to dig it out.
The creek is too deep to cross here. Solve {count} problems to find a shallow spot.
Thick fog rolled in! Solve {count} problems to find the trail markers.
The truck needs gas! Solve {count} problems to reach the next gas station.
detourCleared: Back on the road! Nice driving.
You did it! The road is clear again.
setback: That was a bumpy wander! Let's drive back to the last flag and try again. You can do it!
No problem! Every driver takes a wrong turn sometimes. Back to the last flag we go!

denali: Denali is in Alaska and has the tallest mountain in North America, over 20,000 feet tall.
Grizzly bears, moose, caribou, wolves and Dall sheep all live in the park.
It is the only national park with working sled dogs, who patrol it in winter.
gates-of-the-arctic: Gates of the Arctic is in Alaska and lies completely north of the Arctic Circle.
It has no roads or trails, so visitors arrive by small plane or on foot.
One of the biggest caribou herds in North America roams across the park.
glacier-bay: Glacier Bay is in Alaska, where giant glaciers drop icebergs right into the sea.
Humpback whales, sea otters, harbor seals and puffins live in and around the bay.
Its glaciers shrank back about 48 miles, one of the fastest glacier retreats ever recorded.
katmai: Katmai is in Alaska and is famous for brown bears catching salmon at a waterfall.
Every fall, people vote online for the fattest bear during Fat Bear Week.
A huge volcano eruption buried its Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes in ash.
kenai-fjords: Kenai Fjords is in Alaska and has a giant ice field that feeds nearly 40 glaciers.
Boat tours spot orcas, humpback whales, sea lions and puffins in the fjords.
At Exit Glacier, trail signs show how far the ice has shrunk back over time.
kobuk-valley: Kobuk Valley is in Alaska and has Arctic sand dunes up to 100 feet high.
Hundreds of thousands of caribou cross the Kobuk River every spring and fall.
People have hunted caribou at one river crossing here for about 9,000 years.
lake-clark: Lake Clark is in Alaska and has two active volcanoes, each over 10,000 feet tall.
Brown bears eat clams and grassy plants along the park's coast.
Richard Proenneke built a log cabin here by hand and lived in it about 30 years.
wrangell-st-elias: Wrangell-Saint Elias is in Alaska and is the largest national park in the US.
Mount Saint Elias is over 18,000 feet tall, the second-highest peak in the US.
Kennecott is an old copper-mining town with a giant red mill 14 stories tall.
channel-islands: Channel Islands is in California and is made of five islands out in the ocean.
A small island fox lives here and nowhere else on Earth.
Painted Cave is one of the largest sea caves in the world.
death-valley: Death Valley is in California and Nevada and once hit 134 degrees Fahrenheit, Earth's hottest ever.
Badwater Basin is the lowest point in North America, 282 feet below sea level.
At the Racetrack, rocks slide across a dry lake bed on thin ice.
joshua-tree: Joshua Tree is in California and is named for its twisted yucca trees, called Joshua trees.
Two different deserts, one cooler and one hotter, meet inside the park.
Giant piles of boulders make it one of the world's top places for rock climbing.
kings-canyon: Kings Canyon is in California and has one of the deepest canyons in the US.
In places, the canyon is over 8,000 feet deep.
The giant General Grant Tree is known as the Nation's Christmas Tree.
lassen-volcanic: Lassen Volcanic is in California and has all four types of volcanoes.
Lassen Peak is one of the largest plug-dome volcanoes in the world, over 10,000 feet tall.
Boiling mud pots and steaming vents bubble beside a boardwalk trail.
pinnacles: Pinnacles is in California and has rocky spires left from an ancient volcano.
Visitors explore dark caves made of boulders wedged in narrow canyons, so bring a flashlight.
Endangered California condors have been released back into the wild here.
redwood: Redwood is in California and has the tallest trees on Earth.
Its coast redwoods grow over 350 feet tall, and the tallest one is a secret.
Herds of Roosevelt elk graze in the meadows and along the beaches.
sequoia: Sequoia is in California and has the General Sherman Tree, the largest tree on Earth.
The Giant Forest is home to thousands of giant sequoia trees.
You can climb about 350 steps to the top of Moro Rock, a granite dome.
yosemite: Yosemite is in California and is famous for the giant rocks El Capitan and Half Dome.
Yosemite Falls is over 2,400 feet tall, one of the tallest waterfalls in North America.
Mariposa Grove has more than 500 giant sequoia trees.
american-samoa: American Samoa is a US territory with the only US national park south of the equator.
Big fruit bats called flying foxes fly around during the day.
Some of the healthiest coral reefs in US waters make it great for snorkeling.
crater-lake: Crater Lake is in Oregon and is the deepest lake in the US, almost 2,000 feet.
Its bright blue water fills the bowl of a volcano that collapsed about 7,700 years ago.
Wizard Island is a small volcano cone that pokes up out of the lake.
haleakala: Haleakala is on Maui in Hawaii, where people watch the sun rise above the clouds.
Its summit is over 10,000 feet high, with a huge crater full of cinder cones.
The rare silversword plant and the nene, Hawaii's state bird, live here.
hawaii-volcanoes: Hawaii Volcanoes is in Hawaii and has Kilauea, one of the most active volcanoes on Earth.
Mauna Loa, also in the park, is the largest active volcano on Earth.
You can walk through a lava tube, a tunnel made by flowing lava.
mount-rainier: Mount Rainier is in Washington and is a tall volcano over 14,000 feet high.
It has more glacier ice than any other mountain in the lower 48 states.
Paradise has wildflowers in summer and is one of the snowiest places on Earth in winter.
north-cascades: North Cascades is in Washington and has more than 300 glaciers.
Its jagged, rugged peaks are nicknamed the American Alps.
Diablo Lake is bright turquoise because of fine rock dust from glaciers.
olympic: Olympic is in Washington and has icy mountains, rainforests and wild beaches all in one park.
The Hoh Rain Forest is full of mossy trees and is super wet.
Its beaches have tall sea stacks and tide pools to explore.
arches: Arches is in Utah and has over 2,000 natural stone arches.
Delicate Arch is so famous that it is shown on Utah license plates.
Landscape Arch stretches about 300 feet, one of the longest arches in the world.
big-bend: Big Bend is in Texas and has a whole mountain range, the Chisos Mountains, inside it.
Santa Elena Canyon has rock walls 1,500 feet tall rising straight up from the Rio Grande.
More than 450 kinds of birds can be found in Big Bend.
bryce-canyon: Bryce Canyon is in Utah and has more hoodoos, tall thin rock spires, than anywhere else.
Paiute stories say the hoodoos are Legend People who were turned to stone.
Bryce Canyon is not really a canyon but a set of natural rock bowls called amphitheaters.
canyonlands: Canyonlands is in Utah and has a high, flat mesa called Island in the Sky.
The Needles are colorful sandstone spires that poke up toward the sky.
The Great Gallery has life-size rock paintings made by ancient people.
capitol-reef: Capitol Reef is in Utah and has a wrinkle in the Earth nearly 100 miles long.
Some white rock domes there look like the dome of the US Capitol building.
Visitors can pick fruit from old orchards and eat fresh pies there.
carlsbad-caverns: Carlsbad Caverns is in New Mexico and has one of the biggest cave rooms in North America.
Hundreds of thousands of bats fly out of the cave at dusk in the warm months.
Most of its over 119 caves were dissolved out of an ancient reef by acid.
grand-canyon: The Grand Canyon is in Arizona and is about a mile deep and up to 18 miles wide.
The canyon stretches 277 miles along the Colorado River.
Rafting trips down the river through the canyon can take one to three weeks.
great-basin: Great Basin is in Nevada and has trees nearly 5,000 years old, among the oldest on Earth.
Wheeler Peak is over 13,000 feet tall and has a small glacier.
Lehman Caves is a marble cave full of rare rock formations called shields.
guadalupe-mountains: Guadalupe Mountains is in Texas and has Guadalupe Peak, the highest point in Texas.
The mountains hold an ancient fossil reef about 265 million years old.
El Capitan is a sheer limestone cliff that rises high above the desert.
petrified-forest: Petrified Forest is in Arizona and has ancient logs that turned into colorful stone.
These stone logs are about 218 million years old.
Fossils of early dinosaurs, like Chindesaurus, have been found there.
saguaro: Saguaro is in Arizona and has giant saguaro cactuses that grow over 40 feet tall.
A saguaro cactus can live 150 years or more.
Saguaros grow only in the Sonoran Desert and bloom in May and June.
white-sands: White Sands is in New Mexico and has the world's biggest dunes of white gypsum sand.
Kids can zoom down the dunes on plastic sleds shaped like saucers.
Fossil human footprints found there are more than 20,000 years old.
zion: Zion is in Utah and has towering red and cream cliffs along the Virgin River.
In the Narrows, hikers wade up a river through a skinny slot canyon.
A road in the park goes through a tunnel more than a mile long.
cuyahoga-valley: Cuyahoga Valley is in Ohio and has Brandywine Falls, a 60-foot waterfall.
You can ride a scenic train one way and bike back on the Towpath Trail.
Beaver Marsh is full of wildlife, and the Ledges are cliffs of sandstone.
gateway-arch: Gateway Arch is in Missouri and is the tallest arch in the world, at 630 feet.
Little pod-shaped tram cars ride up inside the arch to the top.
It is the smallest of all the national parks.
indiana-dunes: Indiana Dunes is in Indiana and has tall sand dunes and beaches on Lake Michigan.
One of its sand dunes slowly moves inland several feet every year.
More than 1,100 kinds of native plants grow in the park.
isle-royale: Isle Royale is an island park in Michigan where wolves and moose live.
Scientists there run the world's longest-running study of wolves and moose.
Ten big shipwrecks lie in the cold, clear water of Lake Superior.
voyageurs: Voyageurs is in Minnesota and is a park of big lakes along the Canadian border.
Long ago, fur traders called voyageurs paddled canoes through these waters.
Its dark skies can show the northern lights, and winter brings roads made of ice.
badlands: Badlands is in South Dakota and is full of striped rock towers and spires.
Its rocks hold fossils of ancient mammals like early horses, rhinos, and saber-toothed cats.
Bison, bighorn sheep, prairie dogs, and rare black-footed ferrets live here.
black-canyon-of-the-gunnison: Black Canyon of the Gunnison is in Colorado and is a super deep, narrow canyon.
Its steep walls let only about 33 minutes of sunlight reach parts of the bottom each day.
The Painted Wall is the tallest cliff in Colorado, at 2,250 feet high.
glacier: Glacier National Park is in Montana and is nicknamed the Crown of the Continent.
Mountain goats, bighorn sheep, and grizzly bears live in the park.
The Going-to-the-Sun Road winds 50 miles up and over the mountains.
grand-teton: Grand Teton is in Wyoming, where giant mountains rise straight up from the valley floor.
The tallest peak, called Grand Teton, is 13,775 feet high.
Moose, bison, elk, pronghorn, and bears all live in the park.
great-sand-dunes: Great Sand Dunes is in Colorado and has the tallest sand dunes in North America.
The tallest one, Star Dune, rises about 750 feet high.
In late spring, Medano Creek sends waves across the sand, like a beach in the mountains.
mesa-verde: Mesa Verde is in Colorado, where Ancestral Puebloan people built homes right in the cliffs.
Cliff Palace is the biggest cliff home in North America, with about 150 rooms.
On some tours, you climb ladders and go through tunnels to reach the cliff homes.
rocky-mountain: Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado has more than 60 peaks over 12,000 feet tall.
Trail Ridge Road climbs to 12,183 feet, one of the highest paved roads in the US.
In fall, male elk make loud bugling calls that echo across Moraine Park.
theodore-roosevelt: Theodore Roosevelt National Park, in North Dakota, is the only national park named directly after a person.
Bison, wild horses, elk, and whole towns of prairie dogs live here.
Theodore Roosevelt once had cattle ranches here, and you can visit his cabin.
wind-cave: Wind Cave, in South Dakota, was the first cave in the world to become a national park.
The cave seems to breathe, with wind blowing in or out of its entrance.
It has most of the world's known boxwork, thin rock shaped like a honeycomb.
yellowstone: Yellowstone is in Wyoming, Montana and Idaho and was the first national park in the world.
It has more than half of the world's geysers, including the famous Old Faithful.
Bison, elk, grizzly bears, and wolves roam its valleys.
acadia: Acadia is in Maine and was the first national park east of the Mississippi River.
For part of the year, Cadillac Mountain is among the first US places to see sunrise.
It has 45 miles of gravel carriage roads with stone bridges, and no cars allowed.
biscayne: Biscayne is in Florida, and about 95 percent of the park is water.
It protects part of the only living coral barrier reef in the continental US.
Divers can explore a trail of shipwrecks under the water.
congaree: Congaree is in South Carolina and protects a huge, very old forest that often floods.
Some of the tallest trees in eastern North America grow here.
In late spring, fireflies here flash their lights all at the same time.
dry-tortugas: Dry Tortugas is a park of islands about 70 miles west of Key West, Florida.
Fort Jefferson is the biggest all-brick fort in the Americas, built with about 16 million bricks.
Tortugas means turtles in Spanish, and you can snorkel with sea turtles right off the beach.
everglades: The Everglades, in Florida, is the only place where alligators and crocodiles live side by side.
Its River of Grass is a slow sheet of water flowing across a sawgrass prairie.
Florida panthers, manatees, turtles, and wading birds live here too.
great-smoky-mountains: Great Smoky Mountains, in Tennessee and North Carolina, is called the Salamander Capital of the World.
About 1,900 black bears live in the park.
Cades Cove is a valley with old cabins, churches, and lots of wildlife.
hot-springs: Hot Springs is in Arkansas, right in the middle of a city also named Hot Springs.
Its spring water is about 143 degrees Fahrenheit and fell as rain about 4,000 years ago.
You can fill bottles with hot spring water at public fountains.
mammoth-cave: Mammoth Cave is in Kentucky and is the longest known cave system in the world.
About 426 miles of its passages have been mapped, and the number keeps growing.
Frozen Niagara is a rock formation that looks like a frozen waterfall.
new-river-gorge: New River Gorge is in West Virginia and is the newest national park.
Its giant steel arch bridge stands 876 feet above the river.
Despite its name, the New River may be one of the oldest rivers in North America.
shenandoah: Shenandoah is in Virginia, and Skyline Drive runs 105 miles along the Blue Ridge Mountains.
About 100 miles of the famous Appalachian Trail go through the park.
In October, the forest bursts with bright fall colors.
virgin-islands: Virgin Islands National Park covers about 60 percent of Saint John, an island in the Caribbean.
Trunk Bay has an underwater snorkeling trail you can swim along.
Snorkelers can swim with sea turtles, especially at Maho Bay.
